overview.text: For a one-variable polynomial, the degree is the greatest exponent attached to a term with a nonzero coefficient; when written in standard form, this is the exponent in the leading term. For example, 4x^5 − 2x^2 + 7 has degree 5, even though powers 4 and 3 are missing. Degree gives a bound on a polynomial’s distinct roots: a degree-n polynomial cannot have more than n. More precisely, the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra says a nonzero polynomial of degree n > 0 has exactly n complex roots when repetitions are counted by multiplicity. Thus, some roots may repeat, and some may be nonreal.

key_facts.text: To find the degree, identify the greatest exponent with a nonzero coefficient. In 5t^5 − 2t^3 + 7t, the degree is 5.
Writing terms in descending powers is standard, but the degree is determined by the highest power even if the polynomial is written in another order.
If r is a root, then (x − r) is a factor; dividing by that factor leaves a polynomial whose degree is one less.
A nonzero degree-n polynomial has exactly n complex roots when counted with multiplicity. Repeated roots count more than once, and roots can be nonreal.
Because repeated roots count multiple times, a degree-n polynomial can have fewer than n distinct roots, but not more.
